questions.prompt: Which of these expressions are TRUE (non-zero) in C?
questions.explain: In C, 0 is false and every other value is true. `-1` and `!0` (which is 1) are non-zero. The character constant `'0'` is the ASCII code 48, also non-zero. `NULL` is a null pointer, i.e. zero.
option_notes: Zero is the only false integer value.
Any non-zero value is true, negatives included.
`'0'` is the character whose code is 48, not the number 0.
A null pointer compares equal to 0, so it is false.

questions.prompt: In C, a false value is {{0}}; any other value is true.
questions.explain: There is no mandatory boolean type before C99 (and even `<stdbool.h>` only provides `bool`, `true`=1 and `false`=0 on top of integers).

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (To which `if` does the `else` belong?)
questions.explain: An `else` belongs to the NEAREST `if`, whatever the indentation says. Here `a` is true, `b` is false, so the inner else runs. Use braces to make this explicit.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (There is no `break`.)
questions.explain: Execution enters at `case 2` and CONTINUES through `case 3` (fall-through) until the `break`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (A `default` can be in the middle.)
questions.explain: 7 matches no case, so execution jumps to `default`, and with no `break` it falls through into `case 1`.
The conditions are tested in order; the first true one runs and the rest are skipped.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (`=` or `==`?)
questions.explain: `a = 0` is an ASSIGNMENT whose value is 0 (false), so the else branch runs (and `a` is now 0). `gcc -Wall` warns about assignments in conditions.

questions.prompt: Which type cannot be used as the controlling expression of a `switch`?
questions.explain: A `switch` selects among integer constants: `int`, `char`, enums. Floating-point values and strings are not allowed.
option_notes: Allowed: a char is an integer.
Allowed: an enum value is an integer.

questions.prompt: Is `if (x == 1 || 2)` a correct way to test whether `x` is 1 or 2?
questions.explain: It means `(x == 1) || (2)`, and the non-zero `2` is true. Write `x == 1 || x == 2`.
options: No: it is always true because `2` alone is true
No: it is a syntax error
option_notes: It compiles, but it does not do what it seems.

questions.explain: `x > 3 && x < 10` and `x == 5 || x == 6` are true; `!(x == 5)` is false; 5 is odd so `x % 2 == 1` is true.
